event: Christians are the largest, most widespread non-Muslim minority in Ottoman Palestine — bigger than the Jews. Gaza's Christians are ~25% of the city (the largest single minority community anywhere); Jerusalem's surpass the Jews by 1553-4. A rooted, multi-town population, three centuries before any great-power patron.

event: The Franciscan Custody of the Holy Land is established — the enduring Latin institutional anchor in Palestine.

event: The French Capitulations make France the recognized protector of Catholics across the Ottoman lands — the oldest of the great-power patronage links, and the lever Christians had that Jews and Samaritans did not.

event: Christians live under the same dhimmi extraction as the Jews — jizya, sumptuary distinction — overlaid with the chronic Holy-Places Status Quo disputes between the Greek-Orthodox and Latin clergy.

Under the Egyptian occupation (Ibrahim Pasha), Christians — and, to a lesser extent, Jews — gain de-facto equality with Muslims: seats on the local meclis, entry to the civil service, the right to build and repair churches, and exemption from conscription. The first European consulates open in Jerusalem and Damascus and missionary work is permitted. The pre-Tanzimat equality window — and the very resentment that fed the 1840 anti-Christian backlash.

event: In the peasant revolt against Ibrahim Pasha, Bethlehem's Muslim quarter is destroyed and the Christians are caught in the upheaval — the shared pre-Tanzimat exposure to state-collapse violence.

On the Egyptian withdrawal, a wave of intense anti-Christian — and, to some extent, anti-Jewish — violence sweeps the country: the Muslim backlash against the pro-Christian Egyptian regime and against the Hatt-i Şerif's new doctrine of equality before the law.

event: The great anti-Christian massacres — centered in Damascus and Mount Lebanon, NOT Palestine proper, though panic reigned among the Christians of Galilee. Aqil Agha, the strongman of Galilee, undertook to protect its Christians and Jews (Nazareth especially); Schölch judges that in Palestine itself 'complete tranquillity prevailed' and no Christian was harmed. The flip side of great-power-proxy prestige: the same patronage that drove Christian growth made them targets.

event: The constitutional-revolution civic moment: Muslims, Christians and Jews articulated a shared Ottoman citizenship — 'liberty, equality, fraternity' — a brief inter-communal fraternity running alongside (and against) the hardening nationalisms.

event: The Arab cultural revival (nahda) — disproportionately Christian-led. Figures like Butrus al-Bustani (b. 1819, 'a Christian Arab' of Lebanon) built the Arabic literary-intellectual awakening that became the seedbed of later Arab nationalism.

event: Christian civic life from the inside: the oud-player and civil servant Wasif Jawhariyyeh's memoir captures a festive, cross-communal late-Ottoman and Mandate Jerusalem — Christians, Muslims and Jews sharing music, cafés and one another's feasts.
src: Tamari & Nassar, The Storyteller of Jerusalem 2014

passages.text: Throughout his Ottoman years, and beyond in his adult career, Wasif saw himself as a musician and oud player above all else. When he sought employment in various government and municipal authorities, it was only to survive and release himself to his passionate obsession— the oud—and the company of men and women who shared his vision.
